nodes.label: The Abbasid Revolution wins
nodes.full: Abu Muslim's Khurasani army beats the last Umayyad at the Zab in 750, and the Abbasid line takes the caliphate in the name of 'the family of the Prophet' — the event this folio picks up the morning after.

nodes.label: Talas — Chinese papermakers captured
nodes.full: An Arab-Turkic force beats a Tang army at the Talas river in 751; among the prisoners, tradition holds, were Chinese papermakers whose craft was carried to Samarqand and then Baghdad.
nodes.src: background — see the caliphate-632-750 folio; Bloom, "Paper Before Print" (2001)

nodes.label: Al-Saffah and al-Mansur
nodes.full: Al-Saffah, proclaimed at Kufa in 749, presided over the killing of the Umayyad house. His brother al-Mansur then made the dynasty permanent: he had the revolution's own general Abu Muslim executed (755), crushed the Alid revolt of Muhammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya (762), and in 762 laid out the round administrative capital of Baghdad.

nodes.label: Al-Mahdi
nodes.full: Al-Mahdi spent his reign building Abbasid legitimacy: a campaign of inquisition against Manichaean 'heresy' (zandaqa), lavish patronage of hadith scholars and the pilgrimage, a forced tribute from Byzantium, and the naming of both his sons as heirs in sequence — a decision that later produced civil war.

nodes.label: Harun al-Rashid and the Barmakids
nodes.full: For seventeen years the Barmakid family of viziers ran the empire's finances and patronage; in 803 Harun destroyed them overnight, executing Ja'far and jailing the rest. Harun then split the succession between al-Amin (Baghdad) and al-Ma'mun (Khurasan) and had the arrangement sworn to at Mecca.
nodes.src: al-Tabari; Kennedy, "The Court of the Caliphs" (2004)

nodes.label: The war of al-Amin and al-Ma'mun
nodes.full: The two brothers went to war within a year of Harun's death. Al-Ma'mun's Khurasani army under Tahir besieged and stormed Baghdad in a year-long siege (812-13) that wrecked the round city; al-Amin was caught fleeing and killed. Al-Ma'mun then ruled from Merv until 819.

nodes.label: Al-Ma'mun
nodes.full: Al-Ma'mun sponsored the translation of Greek science, campaigned repeatedly against Byzantium, and in 817 named the Shia imam Ali al-Rida his heir — a gesture Baghdad rejected and his heir's death ended. In his last months he imposed the doctrine of the created Quran on the scholars by inquisition.

nodes.label: Al-Mu'tasim and al-Wathiq
nodes.full: Al-Mu'tasim built a personal army of enslaved Turks and, in 836, moved the entire government to a new city, Samarra, to house them apart from a resentful Baghdad. He stormed the Byzantine city of Amorion (838) and crushed Babak's twenty-year revolt. His son al-Wathiq kept the mihna in force.

nodes.label: Al-Mutawakkil
nodes.full: Al-Mutawakkil abandoned the mihna (849), aligned the caliphate with the traditionist scholars, and moved against dissent: he demolished the shrine of Husayn at Karbala (850) and tightened restrictions on Christians and Jews. His own Turkish guard, with his son, murdered him in 861.

nodes.label: Four caliphs in nine years
nodes.full: Between al-Mutawakkil's murder and 870, the Turkish troops raised and killed four caliphs over pay and faction. The government stopped functioning, the provinces stopped remitting, and the dynasty came as close to ending as it would until the Mongols.

nodes.label: Al-Mu'tamid and the regency of al-Muwaffaq
nodes.full: The caliph al-Mu'tamid reigned; his brother al-Muwaffaq ruled. As regent and commander, al-Muwaffaq broke the Zanj revolt in a hard amphibious campaign (883), checked the Saffarids, and rebuilt an army.

nodes.label: Al-Mu'tadid and al-Muktafi
nodes.full: The last real Abbasid recovery: the court returned permanently to Baghdad, some provinces were pulled back into the fold, the bureaucracy was rebuilt and the finances briefly balanced. It did not survive the reigns of these two competent rulers.

nodes.label: Al-Muqtadir
nodes.full: Enthroned at thirteen, deposed twice and finally killed by his own troops, al-Muqtadir presided over twenty-four years in which his mother and her officials ran the government, viziers were appointed for the cash they could raise, and the Qarmatians carried the Black Stone out of Mecca.

nodes.label: The amir al-umara and the Buyid entry
nodes.full: With the treasury empty the caliphs handed real power to a 'commander of commanders' — held in turn by Ibn Ra'iq, the Turk Bajkam, the Baridi tax-farmers and the Hamdanids. Al-Radi (d. 940) was the last caliph to lead the Friday prayer himself. In 945 the Buyids marched in and made the office a pension.

nodes.label: The Abbasids turn on the family of Ali
nodes.full: The revolution had risen for 'the family of the Prophet'; the Abbasids then spent decades hunting the Alid branch of it. Muhammad 'the Pure Soul' and his brother Ibrahim rose and were killed in 762-63; the Fakhkh massacre followed in 786; survivors founded the Zaydi Shia states of Tabaristan and Yemen.

nodes.label: The siege of Baghdad
nodes.full: Tahir's Khurasani army blockaded the capital for more than a year. Catapults levelled the palaces and the round city, mercenary bands and the city poor fought street by street, and the siege ended with al-Amin caught trying to slip away by boat and beheaded.

nodes.label: Babak and the Khurramiyya
nodes.full: Babak's revolt, under a faith mixing older Iranian religion with social levelling, held the mountains of Azerbaijan for twenty years and destroyed several Abbasid armies. Al-Afshin finally took Babak's fortress and sent him to be executed at Samarra in 838.

nodes.label: Harun's raids and the sack of Amorion
nodes.full: Harun campaigned against Byzantium almost every year, forcing a humiliating tribute on Nikephoros I in 806. In 838 al-Mu'tasim answered a Byzantine raid on Zibatra by storming Amorion, one of the empire's great cities, and enslaving its population. It was the last such Abbasid victory.

nodes.label: Lalakaon — the tide turns
nodes.full: A Byzantine army trapped and destroyed the raiding force of Umar al-Aqta, emir of Melitene, killing him. It ended the era of deep Muslim raids into Anatolia and opened the Byzantine counter-offensive, while the caliphate could no longer field a frontier army.

nodes.label: The Zanj Revolt
nodes.full: The enslaved East African labourers of the salt flats rose under Ali ibn Muhammad, built a fortified state in the marshes, sacked Basra in 871, minted their own coins, and held out for fourteen years, at one point eighty kilometres from Baghdad.

nodes.label: The Saffarid march on Baghdad
nodes.full: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth, a coppersmith's apprentice from Sistan who had conquered an empire across Iran, marched on Baghdad in 876 and was beaten fifty miles short of it. A provincial adventurer had come closer to seizing the caliphate than anyone since the revolution.

nodes.label: The Qarmatians and the humiliation of the Hajj
nodes.full: From their state in eastern Arabia the Qarmatians ambushed pilgrim caravans, sacked Basra (923) and Kufa, and in 930 stormed Mecca during the Hajj, massacred the pilgrims, and carried off the Black Stone. The Abbasid government ended up paying them an annual subsidy.

nodes.label: The wars of the amir al-umara
nodes.full: For a decade Baghdad was fought over by Ibn Ra'iq, the Turk Bajkam, the Baridi tax-farmers of Basra, the Hamdanids of Mosul and finally the Buyids, while the caliph in his palace was a token each of them needed and none of them obeyed.

nodes.label: The vizierate and the diwans
nodes.full: The Abbasids revived the Sasanian model: a wazir as head of government (the Barmakids made the office), a set of specialised bureaus, and a large professional secretary class, the kuttab, most of them of Persian background.

nodes.label: The mihna — the inquisition of the created Quran
nodes.full: Al-Ma'mun and his two successors required judges, witnesses and scholars to profess that the Quran was created, not eternal — a Mu'tazili position — and imprisoned those who refused. Ahmad ibn Hanbal's public resistance made him a hero; al-Mutawakkil abandoned the policy in 849.

nodes.label: The theory of the caliphate is written down
nodes.full: As the caliph's real power drained away, jurists began to define what the office was: a communal obligation to appoint one imam, from Quraysh, to lead prayer, war and justice and enforce the law.

nodes.label: The iqta and the fiscal collapse
nodes.full: Unable to pay the army in cash, the government began assigning soldiers and officials the revenue of estates and districts directly (iqta). It kept the troops fed and hollowed out the central treasury at the same time. By 945 the caliph could not fund a bodyguard.

nodes.label: Al-Mutawakkil's edicts on the dhimmis
nodes.full: Al-Mutawakkil ordered non-Muslims to wear distinctive dress, barred them from state office, and had recently built churches and synagogues demolished. Enforcement was uneven, but the edicts fixed a template of legal subordination that later rulers could revive.

nodes.label: The barid as the caliph's eyes
nodes.full: The postmaster of each province reported directly and secretly to the caliph on the conduct of the governor, the state of the crops, and the price of bread. The barid was as much an intelligence service as a mail system.

nodes.label: The four Sunni schools of law take shape
nodes.full: Abu Hanifa's circle in Kufa, Malik's in Medina, al-Shafi'i (whose Risala founded the theory of the four sources of law), and Ahmad ibn Hanbal's hadith-first school in Baghdad hardened into the four enduring Sunni madhhabs over this century.

nodes.label: Al-Bukhari, Muslim and the canon of hadith
nodes.full: Al-Bukhari (d. 870) and Muslim (d. 875) sifted hundreds of thousands of reported sayings of the Prophet down to a few thousand judged sound. Their two 'Sahih' collections, with four others, became the canonical Sunni hadith corpus.

nodes.label: The Mu'tazila and rational theology
nodes.full: The Mu'tazila built a systematic theology on reason: God's absolute unity (which made the Quran a created thing) and God's justice (which made humans the free authors of their acts). Backed by al-Ma'mun and enforced in the mihna, the school lost state protection under al-Mutawakkil.

nodes.label: Al-Ash'ari and the Sunni theological settlement
nodes.full: Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, trained as a Mu'tazili, broke with the school around 912 and used its own rational methods to defend the traditionalist positions. Ash'arism became the dominant Sunni kalam.

nodes.label: The line of imams ends — the Occultation
nodes.full: When the eleventh imam died in Samarra in 874 leaving no visible heir, his followers held a son existed in hiding, communicating through four successive agents. When the last agent died in 941 without naming a successor, the 'Greater Occultation' began.

nodes.label: The Ismaili da'wa and a third caliphate
nodes.full: A clandestine missionary movement expecting a hidden Ismaili imam spread from Syria across the Maghreb, Yemen, Sind and eastern Arabia. In 909 its leader emerged in Tunisia and was proclaimed the Fatimid caliph — the third simultaneous claimant to the office.

nodes.label: Sufism takes form — al-Junayd and al-Hallaj
nodes.full: Baghdad became the centre of a self-conscious mystical movement: al-Muhasibi's spiritual self-examination, al-Junayd's 'sober' path, and al-Hallaj, executed in the city in 922 after saying 'I am the Truth'.

nodes.label: The geonim, Saadia Gaon and the Karaite schism
nodes.full: The heads (geonim) of the Babylonian rabbinic academies were the supreme authorities for Jews across the Islamic world. Saadia Gaon (d. 942) translated the Bible into Arabic and wrote the first Jewish systematic theology; against him stood the scripturalist Karaites.

nodes.label: Samarra and the spiral minaret
nodes.full: For fifty-six years the caliphate governed from a strip city forty kilometres long on the Tigris. Its Great Mosque was the largest in the world, fronted by a free-standing spiral ramp-minaret (the Malwiya).

nodes.label: The Samarra stucco style spreads the empire over
nodes.full: Samarra's palace decorators developed a moulded stucco of endlessly repeating abstract, slant-cut vegetal forms — the 'beveled style' — that could be cast in quantity. Carried by craftsmen, it turns up from Egypt to Central Asia.

nodes.label: Paper, the warraqs and the book trade
nodes.full: A paper mill was working in Baghdad by the 790s, and within a lifetime cheap paper had displaced papyrus and parchment for everyday use. A whole trade of stationer-copyists (warraqun) grew up around the mosque.

nodes.label: Adab prose — al-Jahiz and the translated wisdom
nodes.full: Ibn al-Muqaffa turned the Persian mirror-for-princes and the Indian animal fables into Arabic before his execution around 756. Al-Jahiz then made Arabic prose into an instrument for everything, founding the genre of adab.

nodes.label: The poetry of the 'moderns'
nodes.full: A generation of poets broke with the desert conventions of the ode: Abu Nuwas made wine and the love of boys his subject; Abu Tammam and al-Buhturi pursued dense rhetorical figures. Arabic poetry became urban, personal and self-aware.

nodes.label: The classical and the romantic schools of song
nodes.full: The Abbasid court sustained a full art-music culture around the singing-girls and the master singers. Ishaq al-Mawsili defended a 'classical' fidelity against the freer style of Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi — the first documented debate about musical authenticity.

nodes.label: The Translation Movement
nodes.full: Over two centuries, sustained by caliphs, viziers and private patrons, nearly the entire surviving corpus of Greek philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy was translated into Arabic, mostly through Syriac and mostly by Christian scholars.

nodes.label: Al-Khwarizmi — algebra and the numerals
nodes.full: Al-Khwarizmi's book on 'restoration and balancing' (al-jabr) founded algebra as a discipline; another work introduced the Indian decimal place-value numerals and zero. His name, Latinised, became 'algorithm'.

nodes.label: Al-Kindi — the philosopher of the Arabs
nodes.full: Al-Kindi supervised translations, argued that philosophy and revelation reach the same truth, and wrote on metaphysics, optics, medicine, music and the cryptanalytic technique of frequency analysis.

nodes.label: Al-Razi and the Baghdad hospital
nodes.full: Al-Razi (Rhazes) directed hospitals at Rayy and Baghdad, kept detailed case notes, wrote the first clinical description distinguishing smallpox from measles, and compiled the vast 'Comprehensive Book' of medicine.

nodes.label: Al-Ma'mun measures the Earth
nodes.full: Al-Ma'mun had teams pace out a degree of latitude on the flat Sinjar plain to check the size of the Earth, and set up observatories to correct Ptolemy's star positions. The resulting 'Verified Tables' began the Arabic tradition of observational astronomy.

nodes.label: History and geography become disciplines
nodes.full: Al-Baladhuri wrote the conquests, Ibn Khordadbeh the roads and revenues, al-Ya'qubi a universal history and geography, al-Tabari a year-by-year history of the world, and al-Masudi a discursive survey of everything.

nodes.label: The Brethren of Purity
nodes.full: An anonymous group in Basra produced the 'Epistles of the Brethren of Purity', a 52-part encyclopedia covering mathematics, logic, natural science, psychology and theology in a Neoplatonic and Ismaili-tinged synthesis.

nodes.label: Baghdad and the instruments of finance
nodes.full: Baghdad may have held close to a million people by 900, the largest city outside China. Its money-changers (sarrafun) developed a real banking system — deposit accounts, the transfer order (the 'sakk'), and the bill of exchange (suftaja).

nodes.label: The Indian Ocean trade at its height
nodes.full: Baghdad's demand pulled the western Indian Ocean into its most intense phase of long-distance trade — dhows sailing from the Gulf to Guangzhou for silk and porcelain, to East Africa for gold and slaves, to India for pepper.

nodes.label: The Sawad — the granary and its decline
nodes.full: The irrigated land between the Tigris and Euphrates was the caliphate's single largest revenue source. Its yield fell from over-taxation, canal neglect, salinisation, and the devastation of the Zanj war — the decline of the Sawad was the decline of the Abbasid state.

nodes.label: The treasury goes bankrupt
nodes.full: Under al-Muqtadir the government's spending — an enormous court, an unpayable army, provincial revolts — outran a revenue base the provinces were no longer remitting. Viziers were appointed and imprisoned for the money they could raise; the coinage was debased.

nodes.label: The dirham flows north — the Rus trade
nodes.full: Hundreds of thousands of Abbasid and Samanid silver dirhams have been dug up in Russia, the Baltic and Scandinavia — payment for the furs, amber and slaves the Rus and Volga Bulgars traded south.

nodes.label: The paper and sugar industries
nodes.full: Two new manufacturing industries scaled up under the caliphate: paper, initially concentrated in Baghdad and Samarqand, and cane sugar, refined in Khuzistan and Egypt with hydraulic mills. Both were export goods that would later travel to Europe.

nodes.label: The paper technology transfer
nodes.full: Paper-making — a Chinese technique, said to have been learned from prisoners taken at Talas in 751 — was established at Samarqand and then Baghdad, adapted to use linen and hemp rag rather than mulberry bark.

nodes.label: The Banu Musa and the Book of Ingenious Devices
nodes.full: The three sons of Musa ibn Shakir, patrons and geometers at al-Ma'mun's court, compiled the 'Kitab al-Hiyal' — a hundred devices using siphons, floats, valves and crank mechanisms, including the earliest known feedback-control systems.

nodes.label: The astrolabe workshop
nodes.full: Abbasid instrument-makers turned the astrolabe from a rare Greek object into a standard, mass-produced brass computer for telling time, finding the qibla, and doing astronomy and astrology.

nodes.label: The hospital as an institution
nodes.full: The bimaristan — a purpose-built, endowed, staffed hospital with separate wards, an out-patient service, a pharmacy and a teaching function — was developed in Abbasid Baghdad, drawing on the older Persian model of Jundishapur.

nodes.label: The Christian and Sabian translators
nodes.full: The Greek sciences reached Arabic largely through non-Muslims: Nestorian Christians like Hunayn ibn Ishaq, who worked from Syriac versions, and the star-worshipping Sabians of Harran like Thabit ibn Qurra, who brought a living Greek mathematical tradition.

nodes.label: Harun al-Rashid and Charlemagne
nodes.full: Frankish and Abbasid embassies exchanged gifts — a water-clock, an elephant named Abul-Abbas, keys to the Holy Sepulchre. The contact was real but minor for Baghdad and large for the Franks.

nodes.label: Ibn Fadlan on the Volga
nodes.full: The caliph al-Muqtadir sent an embassy to the recently converted king of the Volga Bulgars. Its secretary Ibn Fadlan wrote a report describing the Turks, the Bashkirs and a Rus chieftain's ship-cremation funeral.

nodes.label: Manuscript-hunting in Byzantium
nodes.full: Abbasid missions to Byzantium came back with Greek manuscripts as much as with treaties, and the demand may have helped spark the 9th-century Byzantine revival of classical learning.

nodes.label: Three caliphs at once
nodes.full: The Fatimid leader took the title of caliph in Ifriqiya in 909; the Umayyad ruler of al-Andalus answered with his own claim in 929. For the first time three men called themselves the sole legitimate leader of all Muslims simultaneously.

nodes.label: The Darb Zubayda — the pilgrim road
nodes.full: Harun's wife Zubayda paid for the paving, milestones, wells and cisterns of the pilgrim road from Iraq to Mecca, and a water supply for Mecca itself.

nodes.label: The Sasanian model revived
nodes.full: With the centre in Iraq and the state run by Persian secretaries, the caliphate absorbed the political culture of the empire it had replaced: the vizier, elaborate court ceremonial, the veil between ruler and subject, the Persian new-year at court.

nodes.label: The provinces slip away
nodes.full: Governors turned their offices into hereditary dynasties while still sending the Friday prayer in the caliph's name: the Aghlabids in Tunisia (800), the Tahirids then Saffarids and Samanids in the east, the Tulunids in Egypt (868).

nodes.label: The slave-soldier state
nodes.full: Al-Mu'tasim's decision to build his army from enslaved Turks bought from beyond the frontier created a self-reproducing military caste with no roots in the society it ruled. The pattern became the normal way Islamic states raised troops for a thousand years.

nodes.label: Byzantium turns the tide
nodes.full: After Lalakaon in 863 the initiative on the eastern frontier passed to Byzantium. The Macedonian emperors pushed the border east, and by the 940s the reconquests of Crete, Cilicia and Antioch were in sight.

nodes.label: The Buyids take Baghdad
nodes.full: Ahmad ibn Buya, a Daylamite soldier leading a Shia dynasty, marched into Baghdad and took over. He left the Abbasid caliph on his throne, drawing a pension, and ran the state himself with the title 'commander of commanders'.

nodes.label: The ghilman — enslaved soldiers who ruled
nodes.full: Bought as boys from the Turkish steppe, converted, trained together and manumitted into the army, the ghilman owed everything to their commanders and nothing to the society around them. Within thirty years they were choosing and killing caliphs.

nodes.label: The qiyan — the singing-girls as an institution
nodes.full: Trained from childhood in poetry, music and repartee and sold for enormous sums, the qiyan were the most cultivated women of the age and, through the men who competed for them, wielded real influence.

nodes.label: The women who ran the palace
nodes.full: Khayzuran, Harun's mother and a former slave, was effectively co-ruler in the 780s; Zubayda funded the pilgrim road; and Shaghab, mother of al-Muqtadir, directed the government for much of 908-932. The harem was a department of state.

nodes.label: The many slaveries of the Abbasid world
nodes.full: Abbasid slavery was not one condition but several: the East African Zanj worked to death in gangs on the salt flats; the Turkish ghilman rose to command armies; the qiyan and eunuch chamberlains lived at the centre of power.

nodes.label: The People of the Book as a professional elite
nodes.full: For all the legal subordination of the dhimma, Christians dominated medicine and translation, Jews a good part of banking and long-distance trade, and both supplied secretaries to the diwans.

nodes.label: Al-Hallaj and the limits of religious expression
nodes.full: The Sufi al-Hallaj preached in the streets, claimed union with God in words that sounded like a claim to be God, and was flogged, mutilated and hanged after an eleven-year trial tangling political and doctrinal charges.
